dialog.body: Public Works storm line, this is Denise. What's going on?
Hi, yeah, Denise. Okay. So I figured City Hall's closed, it's Saturday, but somebody said there's a storm line that's open, so, here I am. That's you, right? You're the storm line?
That's me. We're staffing it through the weekend because of this storm. What's the problem?
The problem is my mother's basement's got water in it. Again, the street, I mean, not the basement again. The street floods again. The basement's new. Ha, I'm already doing it. Let me start over.
Go ahead, take your time.

Okay. So my mother's house is 701 Thames Street, down the Fifth Ward end, right there by the corner. Overnight Friday into this morning, with the storm, the drain at the corner just, it backed up. Like the water came up out of the grate first. Out of the street drain, into the street, and then it came across and into the house.
Okay. 701 Thames. And you saw it come up out of the grate?

My mother saw it, she was up, she doesn't sleep in a storm. She said it was bubbling up out of the drain like a pot. And then it's coming in the basement windows, and then also up through the floor drain down there, which, I didn't even know a floor drain could go backwards. Well, I knew. I didn't think about it.
How much water are we talking about in the basement?

About three inches. I measured it with, uh, a tape measure. Three inches. It's not finished down there, thank God, it's just the concrete, so it's not like carpet. But the furnace is down there. It's up on blocks, my father set that up years ago, before he passed, and the water got up on the blocks, it got the bottom of it wet. And the washer and dryer, both of those got wet.
Is the furnace still running?

It is, yeah, I work on these, I do HVAC, so I looked at it this morning. It's okay for now. But that's not the point. The point is, Denise, that grate. That corner grate has been packed with leaves since, like, October. You can walk by and see it. Every big rain that corner turns into a lake, and nobody comes. And now it's in the house.
Understood.

So what I want to know, and I'm not trying to yell at you, you didn't do it, but when was that drain last cleaned? Like, actually cleaned. Is there a record of that? Because I don't think anybody's touched it in a year. Maybe more.
Let me look. Hold on one second.
Sure.

[pause] Okay, I'm in the system. I'm not seeing a cleaning logged for that specific basin on this screen. That doesn't mean nobody's been there, the older maintenance stuff isn't all in what I can pull up on a weekend. But I don't have a date to give you.
See, that's what I mean. Nobody knows. Ha. Nobody knows when anybody did anything. Meanwhile my mother's out there with a shop vac at seven in the morning.

I hear you. What I can do right now is log this as a drain backup with water into the house, at the corner by 701 Thames, and put it in for a crew to come look at the grate. With everything from this storm they're running all over the city, but this goes on the list for the next few days.
The next few days. Okay. And if it rains again before that?
Then you call back and tell us, and I'll bump the note. Honestly, the backup with water in a home gets looked at before the ones that are just ponding in the road.

Okay. Okay, that's something. Because this is my mother's house, she's been there almost forty years, she shouldn't be the one out there pulling leaves off a city drain with a rake. Which, by the way, she did. This morning. In the rain.
Please tell her not to do that while it's still running. That water's moving fast at the grate.

You tell her. She won't listen to me. I was over there this morning and she had me hanging a new curtain rod in the front room, in the middle of all this. Like, the basement is a swimming pool, and she's worried about the curtains. I'm up on a chair with a drill and she's out at the corner with a rake. Ha. What was I saying?
You were telling me about the drain.
Right. Right, the drain. So it was the street drain first. I want that written down, that it came up from the street, it's not like our gutters or something. It's the city drain.

I've got it. Water came up from the street catch basin first, then into the basement through the basement windows and the floor drain, about three inches. Furnace on blocks and the washer and dryer got wet. That right?
That's it. That's exactly it.
Can I get your name, and a number in case the crew wants to reach somebody?
Paul Pucci. P-U-C-C-I. And it's my cell, 401-555-0188. Call me, not my mother, she'll be at work Monday anyway and she won't pick up a number she doesn't know.
Paul Pucci, 401-555-0188. Got it. Owner's your mother?
Yeah, Eleanor. Eleanor Pucci.
Okay. It's in. Drain backup, 701 Thames, crew to look at the corner grate in the next few days.
And they'll actually come? Like, a truck shows up? Because I feel like every year we see the leaves sit there and nobody ever, you know.
It's logged with water in a house, so yes, somebody's going out. If you don't see anybody by the middle of the week, call the regular Public Works number Monday and reference today.
Okay. Middle of the week. I'm writing that on my hand. Ha. Okay, thanks, Denise. Sorry for venting at you on a Saturday.
That's what the line's for. Keep your mother off the corner, alright?
I'll try. No promises. Thanks.
